items.title: Seat in Dubai, assets in India: The missing last mile
items.summary: At Dubai Arbitration Week this November, the Registrar of the Dubai International Arbitration Centre (“DIAC”) is reported to have told a panel on India–UAE trade that a draft of the notification the corridor has been waiting for has been prepared. He meant the notification under Section 44(b) of India’s Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (“the Act”). Without it, an award made in Dubai or Abu Dhabi is not a “foreign award” in India and cannot be enforced there, as an award from London, Singapore or Moscow can. That India should issue it has been argued often and well. We take that case as made. Our interest is in three matters the debate tends to pass over: what the award-holder is left with today, how the question looks from New Delhi, and what to do with a Dubai clause in the meantime. A gap in the list, not a verdict on the UAE Section 44 of the Act asks two things of a foreign award. It must arise from an arbitration agreement to which the New York Convention applies, and be made in a territory that the Central Government, “ being satisfied that reciprocal provisions have been made ”, has notified in the Official Gazette. items.title: Delhi High Court quashes criminal defamation case against Senior Advocate Pinaki Misra
items.summary: The Delhi High Court has quashed criminal defamation proceedings initiated against Senior Advocate and former Biju Janata Dal (BJD) Member of Parliament Pinaki Misra for calling a lawyer a “crook”. In an order passed on November 17, Justice Sachin Datta observed that the complainant, advocate Siddhartha Singh, had failed to show that Misra's statement lowered his reputation in the estimation of others. The Court allowed Misra' plea and set aside the summoning order passed by a trial court in April 2019 as well as the complaint filed by Singh. "It is also noticed that the impugned order does not consider the context in which the words were allegedly used by the petitioner and the dismissal of the complaint by the Bar Council of Delhi," the Court said. The case arose from an August 2018 report published by The Economic Times about a complaint filed by Singh before the Bar Council of Delhi, alleging professional misconduct by Misra over a conflict of interest. At the time, Misra was a Lok Sabha MP and chairperson of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Urban Development. Mohanlal was speaking after inaugurating the Mathangi Multimedia Recording Studio, an initiative of Kesari . In his address, he said the publication was founded by Sangh workers who wanted to build a space for journalism and social engagement rooted in patriotism. "The Sangh was fulfilling a cultural responsibility through this endeavour. Only if the nation survives can this culture survive. Kesari has proclaimed this truth loudly and consistently through each of its activities," he said. The RSS, founded in 1925, is a Hindu nationalist organisation and the ideological parent of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Describing Kesari as a symbol of self-respect and patriotism, Mohanlal said the weekly had helped pass on the teachings of "the great civilisation of Bharat" to successive generations. items.title: Sabarimala: Up to Rs 5,000 fine for discarding clothes, waste in Pamba river
items.summary: The Sabarimala season is here, drawing lakhs of devotees to Sabarimala this month, the Pampa River is once again drowning in non-biodegradable garbage at the Pampa and Triveni bathing ghats. Despite multi-language warning boards put up by the government, thousands of pilgrims are ignoring the rules and dumping synthetic clothes, plastic wrappers, and used tissues straight into the water under the guise of Vastra Danam . Vastra Danam is a ritual followed by pilgrims in which devotees abandon their worn clothes in the river, believing it washes away their past sins. The Travancore Devaswom Board assigned Clean Kerala Company Ltd (CKCL) and 30 sanitation workers; however, persistent delays in clearing the ghats have resulted in wet piles of nylon and polyester choking the riverbed. What starts out every morning as a customary dip before the forest walk swiftly devolves into a dense tangle of floating trash and abandoned clothing. As footfall climbs higher each day of the current season, the gap between pilgrim numbers and waste collection is leaving the river basin visibly suffocated. items.title: Rights groups urge sanctions after top UN court finds Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
items.summary: By Edith M. Lederer Rights groups are calling for military and economic sanctions against Myanmar after the United Nations' highest court, in the first ruling of its kind, determined that its government committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation. The International Court of Justice has no power to enforce Thursday's ruling , which orders Myanmar’s military-supported government to allow those who fled the violence to return home safely, to pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide. Myanmar’s government has denied committing genocide, claiming it acted against insurgents, and is considered unlikely to fulfill any of the court’s demands. President Min Aung Hlaing, the former military leader, was in charge of the 2017 operation. The court said evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 100,000 Rohingya. items.title: The history of the persecution of Myanmar’s Rohingya
items.summary: Some 420,000 Rohingya Muslims, a religious and ethnic minority community in Myanmar, have fled to neighboring Bangladesh since August this year. The United Nations has called the Rohingya the world’s most persecuted minority group and described the atrocities by Myanmar’s authorities as “ ethnic cleansing ,” whereby one group removes another ethnic or religious community through violence. But the persecution of the Rohingya is not new. My research on the Rohingya Muslim experience in Myanmar shows that this pattern of persecution goes back to 1948 – the year when the country achieved independence from their British colonizers. Here is their brief history. The legacy of colonialism The British ruled Myanmar (then Burma) for over a century, beginning with a series of wars in 1824 . Colonial policies encouraged migrant labor in order to increase rice cultivation and profits. Many Rohingya entered Myanmar as part of these policies in the 17th century. According to census records , between 1871 to 1911, the Muslim population tripled. The British also promised the Rohingya separate land – a “ Muslim National Area ” – in exchange for support. items.title: How your body clock affects your mental health and ways to keep it in sync
items.summary: Ever wondered why a bad night’s sleep can leave you irritable, anxious or sad? Poor sleep affects our emotions, but its timing also plays a role. Our circadian rhythms are nearly 24-hour cycles that regulate alertness, hormones, body temperature and digestion. Deep inside the brain, a cluster of nerve cells called the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) acts as the body’s master clock. It uses light signals from the eyes to coordinate clocks in other organs, including the brain, liver, heart and gut. When daily routines fall out of sync with this clock, mood can suffer. Research suggests circadian disruption may contribute to mental health challenges. Our internal clock helps regulate hormones, including melatonin and cortisol. Melatonin helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle. Levels stay low during the day, rise in the evening as darkness falls (signalling to the brain that it is time to rest), peak in the middle of the night, and drop off in the morning. Cortisol, which helps us respond to stress, typically rises towards morning. These changes prepare the body for activity and rest, while influencing emotional wellbeing. items.title: Cop31: Why the UN climate summit ended in victory for fossil fuel producing nations
items.summary: The UN’s annual two-week climate summit, Cop31 , has ended in failure. Countries could not find consensus on a final agreement. It is the first such failure in more than 20 years. The summit started relatively smoothly. In fact, the conference agenda was adopted within a few hours on day one, as country parties found nothing objectionable. At the time, this event looked like it might be smooth sailing: another summit simply focused on implementing policies agreed in previous years. But week two became explosive. First, the draft agreement – which if adopted would have been known as the Antalya Accords – conceded that we have failed to keep global temperature rise below 1.5˚C and that the world is entering a period of “overshoot” . Second, oil and gas producing nations fought to keep the root cause of climate change – namely fossil fuels – out of any deal. And they succeeded, as the agreement fell through. items.title: Going to the park once a week or more has a measurable impact on a child’s mental health – new study
items.summary: Child mental health issues have been rising in the UK over the last decade . This was exacerbated by the COVID pandemic and continues to be a concern, particularly around issues such as sedentary lifestyles and excessive screen time. In a new study , colleagues and I have found that visiting a local park regularly had a measurable impact on child mental health . Throughout childhood and through adolescence, children are developing their social and emotional skills. This social-emotional development provides the foundation for good mental health. Failing to reach typical milestones such as developing social skills and friendships provides an indication of a child’s current mental health, as well as their mental health in later life. This means that finding ways to facilitate and encourage healthy social-emotional development is a way to improve child mental health and give them the foundation for good mental health throughout their lives. Having green and natural spaces close to people’s homes is one factor which previous studies have shown is linked with improved child mental health. Wasim @ Wassi v. State of West Bengal and Anr] Justice Chaitali Chatterjee Das dismissed the revision petition filed by the accused Wasim for quashing the charges framed against him by the trial court. The Court observed that altering the charges would negatively impact the trial proceedings. "This Court is of the considered view that if at this threshold stage, charge is altered and a charge for substantially lesser offence is framed there would hardly remain any scope for the prosecution to proceed effectively with the trial in respect of the gravity of the allegation and the role attributed to the petitioner, even if later found some ingredients against the petitioner for commission of grave offence", the Court observed. The Court added that the trial court would be at liberty to examine the necessary evidence and decide the ultimate fate of the prosecution case during the trial.
